body:
Second slice of #180: #109's linear machine, with one human gate and evidence at every step.

```
validated → discovered → previewed → approved → provisioning → canary → health-confirm → active
```

**Before the gate, everything is read-only**, so a failure there simply aborts — there's nothing outside to undo. The preview covers both the plan *and* a shadow poll, and its fingerprint covers both: "the same config that would now fire on forty cards instead of three" is a different thing to approve, and a static plan can't say that.

**The gate refuses two ways.** An approver who doesn't *positively* hold Release authority can't approve — and uncertainty is not approval, since an unconfirmed permission has confirmed nothing. And the approval is bound to the exact preview it was given: if the config or board moved since, the yes describes a world that no longer exists and must be re-taken.

**After the gate nothing asks a human again.** Provisioning is add-only and idempotent, so a failed step leaves the attempt to **resume forward** rather than unwinding the steps that worked, and a step that raises is recorded as evidence rather than crashing the attempt. The canary is one real wake that finishes cleanly — a **no-op wake is sufficient proof**, since it already exercises discovery, the lock, state read/write, GitHub auth and a healthy exit; demanding a dispatch would refuse to activate a project that simply has no pending work. Health confirmation checks the steady state, and an empty set of checks is not a pass.

**Rollback** restores which configuration is selected and never reverses an external effect that already completed. A first activation has nothing to return to, so it stays off: the timer comes out and harmless GitHub labels are deliberately **left in place**, because deleting a label a human may have started using would be a destructive surprise rather than a cleanup. A re-activation returns to the previous record and keeps running on it.

The record accretes the whole audit trail — contract, fingerprints, binding, preview fingerprint, shadow summary, approver and time, provisioning, canary, health — and doubles as the per-wake drift baseline (#108).

## Verification

27 focused tests: read-only aborts, discovery freezing the binding, the preview fingerprint changing with plan *or* behavior, all four gate refusals (no authority, uncertainty, stale fingerprint, no fingerprint), no skipping the gate, provisioning (records what landed, resumes forward, a raising step is evidence), the canary refusing incomplete provisioning, one clean wake being enough, health failure naming the check, an empty check set not passing, the record round-trip, and both rollback paths.

Full suite **1189 pass**, same 2 failures that pre-exist on `master`. Ruff clean, stdlib-only boundary guard green.

Next: the GitHub read/effect adapter — where the port's shape meets real payloads. I'll record real `gh`/GraphQL output first rather than inventing fixtures.

First slice of #180: #110's authorization model, owned by the engine.

**The port no longer decides anything.** It supplied a verdict before; now it supplies one raw fact — the collaborator level GitHub reports — and every judgment about what that means lives in `authorization.py`. An authorization rule is an engine invariant; an adapter shouldn't be trusted to get it right.

- **Two ordered tiers, Work strictly inside Release.** A Release Controller always holds Work authority, so a maintainer is never blocked from a work command — including through the allowlist, where a Release entry also grants Work. Bars and allowlists combine by **union, grant-only**. Defaults are #110's as ordered bars: Work accepts triage and above, Release requires maintain or admin.
- **Three outcomes, and the third carries the weight.** Uncertainty defers and is retried — never granted, never dropped — so a GitHub blip can't silently discard a legitimate `/merge` and an outage can't authorize one. A clean answer in either direction is final.
- **Two easy-to-get-wrong rules, explicit and tested.** `author_association` is only a cheap pre-filter (an `OWNER` association still proves nothing, because only the live level separates the tiers), and the engine's own account is never a controller whatever role it holds. A *missing* association is treated as **unknown rather than "none"**: absence of the shortcut means the lookup decides, not that the commenter is refused.
- **The tier table**, including Release on `/merge review` — the authority to start an auto-progressing publication equals the authority to merge. An extension command carries its declared tier, and an unrecognized tier reads as Release: guessing down would be privilege escalation, guessing up only asks for more proof.

The default policy refuses everyone, because a project that has stated no policy has named nobody who may steer it. The test fixtures now carry an explicit policy, which is why the shared fake gained a `run_wake` helper.

## One thing deferred to the adapter slice

Authorizing a **hand-added ownership label** needs the actor behind the label event, which the port doesn't report yet. That lands with the GitHub adapter, where the actor becomes available. Command authorization is complete here.

## Verification

33 focused tests: the policy slot and its fallbacks, Work⊂Release in both directions and through both allowlists, union/grant-only, every level against both bars, all three outcomes (including unreadable *and* unrecognized levels as uncertain), the pre-filter, the bot, the tier table, extension tiers, and the activation approval gate using the same rule.

Full suite **1162 pass**, same 2 failures that pre-exist on `master`. Ruff clean, stdlib-only boundary guard green.

Next: the activation state machine (#109).

Closes #217

## What was wrong

Deckhand kept raising `stalled` attention for chats whose work was already done, and a restart brought them all straight back.

The classifier runs under `--output-schema src/agentdeck/assistant_output.schema.json`, so that file decides what Codex is *allowed* to answer. It still offered the retired vocabulary `["blocked", "review", "done"]`, while the prompt and `triage.parse_verdict()` moved to `blocked | finished` in a1b154c (19 Jul) without it. Codex therefore could never emit `finished`; whatever it did emit was not in `{blocked, finished}`, so `parse_verdict()` coerced it to `blocked` — and `_STATUS_KIND` maps `blocked` to the warn-coloured `stalled` card.

Evidence from the live assistant checkpoint at the time of the report:

- **69 of 69** cached verdicts had status `blocked`, **zero** `finished`
- their own reasons say otherwise: *"No operator action is required; optionally sanity-check the live behavior"*, *"Work is complete on master at cba49fe"*, *"Work is complete; verify the pinned card in the chat if needed"*
- all 7 cards in the screenshot were `stalled` cards backed by those verdicts, not by a stall or a failed read

This is why the three previous fixes did not stop it: they hardened *suppression* (dismissals across restarts, done markers through GitHub failures, merged-PR contexts across a cold start), while the verdict itself was wrong at the source. A wrong verdict is cached against the session's evidence signature, so it persists until that evidence changes — a restart just makes the whole set visible at once.

## The change

- `assistant_output.schema.json`: `status` enum → `["blocked", "finished"]`.
- `triage.VERDICT_STATUSES` is now the single source of truth for the vocabulary; `parse_verdict()` uses it, and a test asserts the shipped schema offers exactly it and that every status it offers survives parsing uncoerced. The drift cannot silently return.
- Assistant checkpoint v6 → v7. A v6 payload is still restored, minus its verdicts — those were all classified under the stale schema, so restoring them would keep the same chats stalled after the deploy. View, signatures and the complete git contexts (the abb6920 protection against re-raising retired attention on a cold process) are kept.
- `.claude/codebase/deckhand-assistant.md` records the schema/vocabulary invariant.

After this, a finished agent classifies as `finished` → the calmer, lower-priority `finished` card that sinks below real attention, instead of a `stalled` one. Sessions whose PRs all merged stay suppressed by `is_shipped` as before.

## Verification

- `.venv/bin/pytest -q` — 1109 passed. Two failures (`test_spawn_omits_agentdeck_url_without_base`, `test_app_server_enables_live_web_search`) are pre-existing on a clean `master` tree, confirmed by re-running them with the change stashed.
- Both new tests were confirmed red against the old schema/checkpoint behaviour before being made green.
- `.venv/bin/ruff check` on the changed Python files — clean. `git diff --check` — clean.
- Live probing of Codex itself was not possible: the Deckhand Codex account is at its usage limit until 28 Jul (`ERROR: You've hit your usage limit`), which is also the source of the *"Some agents could not be read."* line in the screenshot. The 69/69 checkpoint evidence above is the empirical proof instead.

No visual change — the diff touches no template, stylesheet, static asset or `render.py`. The user-visible effect is which card kind Deckhand produces, which needs a live classifier run to show.
